title: How can you test whether an LLM actually improves strategy selection?
author: Alphanet_dogwalker
selftext:
I'm a researcher at AlphaNet. In our recent research ([https://alphanet.global/agentic-trading-strategy-selection.html](https://alphanet.global/agentic-trading-strategy-selection.html)), LLM agents interpret investor preferences, evaluate candidate strategies and propose allocations. Separate tools run backtests, calculate correlations and check risk constraints; another service handles execution and position management.  
  
The selector works with strategy signals, performance histories and metadata. It doesn't get to inspect the underlying strategy code. The part I'd like outside views on is how to test the contribution of the LLM itself. Say it picks three strategies that fit the user's risk limits. A simple ranking rule and portfolio optimiser might pick a similar combination from the same data. A convincing explanation wouldn't tell you which made the better allocation.  
  
I can see a useful role in turning something vague like “I can tolerate a bad month, but I need access to the money” into constraints the system can check. But once those constraints are fixed, does the LLM still improve the selection?  
  
Has anyone compared the two using the same candidate strategies, information available at the time and risk limits? What decision did the agent change and did that help on subsequent data?

comments.author: Emotional-Breath-838
comments.body:
One of the biggest challenges that we face right now is that everything has changed.  I’ll make a finer point on that but here’s why it’s relevant to your question first. 

When the market changes the game, as I argue below, the backtesting must have an asterisk on it.  What worked when Korea had leverage or when Japan had zero interest rates may not work when both of those are no longer true and oil is over $100/bl. 

Even if you could go back in time, digitally, and find nearly identical macros, you would be deluding yourself that it could reproduce results.  Every trader has AI stock analysis. More retail is in the pool than ever before, even if it’s a fraction.  

Why this time is not like other times…

You have no idea when the US Iran war will end.  You don’t know when the Houthis will stop destroying Saudi pipelines.  You don’t know when the AI capex music will stop and who will be left without a chair.  

The bull market ended.  Not with a pop but a slow release of gas like a thin man’s fart.  It’s not a bear market. It’s more of a koala bear market - going up and down the tree looking to get stoned off of eucalyptus leaves. 

Who will win the midterms in the US? You have no clue. If the Dems win, the last two years of Trump’s tenure will be spent on impeachment trials.  If the GOP wins, what radical transformations do they advance with their perceived mandate? 

Nuclear? 

AI? 

Robotics?

Space? 

Massive infrastructure and grid updates? 

Inflation driving tariffs? 

You have no idea and your strategy may be based on a world that no longer exists.

replies.author: Alphanet_dogwalker
replies.body: That's also why I'd keep a simple selector running alongside it. Both have to deal with the same unfamiliar market. If the LLM's answer is to hold more cash, the baseline needs that option too. Otherwise “better adaptation” might just mean it took less risk. I'd want to separate those before giving the model credit

comments.author: QuanTradin
comments.body:
your own framing has the test in it. freeze the constraint translation step, hand both sides the same candidate set and the same information cutoff, and run the llm selector against a plain ranking rule plus optimiser. anything that lets the two see different constraints is measuring the preference parser instead of the selector.

two things make it harder than it looks. only the disagreement cases carry information, because where the agent and the baseline picked the same three the outcome tells you nothing either way, so your real sample is the subset where it deviated and that shrinks fast. and run the selector several times on identical input before anything else, because if the picks move between runs you have a variance floor, and an edge narrower than that spread is not an edge.

the leak i would worry about most is the metadata. it cannot see the code, so it is reading names, descriptions and histories, and those are usually written or curated after the fact. if the candidate pool is itself made of strategies that survived, the selector will look good for a reason that has nothing to do with selecting.

replies.author: Alphanet_dogwalker
replies.body:
The metadata point is the awkward one. Hiding a strategy's name won't fix a description written after its good run, or a candidate pool that already excludes the failures. We'd need the list and descriptions as they existed at each decision date  
  
Did you find a workable way to reconstruct that history or would you treat this as a forward-only test until enough decisions have accumulated?

replies.author: Alphanet_dogwalker
replies.body:
The candidate-pool point is probably the bigger problem here. If the failed strategies are already gone, the pool has done some of the selecting for you before the LLM even sees it.   
We'd need the old lists and descriptions including the stuff that got dropped. Without those, I would put more weight on running both selectors forward than on a clean-looking historical comparison

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: agreed, a pool that already dropped the losers has done half the selecting. forward is the only clean version, and it's slow, months not days.

comments.author: VisibleBee
comments.body: I would isolate the selector as an intervention: hold the candidate strategies, data cutoff, risk rules, and execution assumptions fixed, then compare the LLM selector with random, rank-based, and rules-only choices on locked walk-forward periods. Report abstention, turnover, overlap, and tail loss, not just return.
